This checklist is not a validated skill score or proof of future profitability. The new observation does not prove the method will fail forever, but it demonstrates how a very small sample’s headline can change abruptly.

text:
Two hypothetical public practice accounts end at $120,000 and $115,000 from $100,000 starts. The first briefly fell to $65,000; the second’s low was $95,000. Ignore costs and cash flows. A return-ranked leaderboard can place the first account above the second without explaining the very different paths used to reach those final values.

Measure each supplied low against the $100,000 start, but do not call it maximum peak-to-trough drawdown without the complete path. Then calculate the gain needed to return from each low to the start. The two accounts have different downside paths even before considering their ending returns. A leaderboard can show one ranking metric without certifying superior decision quality or suitable personal risk.

A learner refreshes a hypothetical position 40 times in an hour without any new evidence. Another schedules two observation sessions and records the same available facts. Compare time spent with useful information gathered. A review schedule can support attention and documentation, but it does not place orders or guarantee results. Consider what would justify checking sooner than planned.

A worksheet imagines an asset worth $100 falling to $80 or rising to $120. No probability is assigned to either branch. A learner averages the two prices and calls $100 the asset’s expected future price. A pair of possibilities can organize thinking, but it is not automatically a complete probabilistic model.

Then compare equal weights as another branch. These are chosen assumptions, not estimates derived from market evidence. A weighted average can summarize such assumptions without guaranteeing that the price will equal the average.

TradeHQ’s quick directional challenge is a reflection exercise, while the deeper questions assess explicit concepts and arithmetic. No future market outcome or calibrated forecasting model is supplied. Keep objective answer checking separate from the discussion of uncertainty. Completing a longer case can contribute one streak day, but it should not fabricate a prediction score or cause automatic trading.

text:
A market order asks to trade at the available price. A limit order sets the highest price you will pay to buy or the lowest price you will accept to sell, and it may go unfilled.

Practice example: If an asset last traded at $50 and the next available sell price is $51, a market buy could fill at $51. A buy limit at $50 would wait for a seller at $50 or less. TradeHQ executes simulated market orders.

text: Spread and Slippage
reason: Enumerated only. Do not treat hashes, tests or static page reading as individual review of this interactive content.

text:
The bid is the best available buy price and the ask is the best available sell price. If the bid is $49.90 and the ask is $50.10, their spread is $0.20.

Slippage is the difference between the expected price and the actual fill. If you expect to buy at $50.10 and fill at $50.25, that is $0.15 of adverse slippage per unit. A last traded price, an available quote and a fill can each be different.

text:
Drawdown measures how far an account has fallen from an earlier peak. If your simulated portfolio reaches $110,000 and then falls to $99,000, the drawdown is $11,000 divided by $110,000, or 10%.

Return and drawdown answer different questions. That same account is down 1% from a $100,000 starting balance while it is down 10% from its peak.

A stop order uses a trigger price. When a standard stop triggers, it becomes a market order and can fill at a different price.

text:
RSI is a momentum oscillator scaled 0–100 measuring speed and change of price moves.

• >70 = overbought (potential pullback)
• <30 = oversold (potential bounce)
• 50 is the midpoint of the scale.

Practice example: If an asset is rising and its RSI moves from 72 to 76, both readings are above the traditional 70 threshold. A strong trend can keep RSI elevated. The readings describe recent momentum, so check the price history before drawing conclusions about a reversal. RSI alone is not a buy/sell signal.

text: Trading Psychology

text:
Trading decisions can be affected by emotion, attention and cognitive bias. Psychology matters, but there is no credible universal percentage that separates psychology from strategy.

The 4 killers:
• FOMO — acting from fear of missing a move without checking an assumption.
• Revenge trading — increasing activity or exposure to recover a loss without reassessing risk.
• Anchoring — refusing to sell because 'I'll wait until it gets back to my entry'.
• Confirmation bias — only reading news that supports your position.

Practice review: Record the original reasoning and compare it with the outcome. Ghost Journal and Revenge Blocker can support a review, but do not cure bias or guarantee disciplined decisions.
